title: A Father Told Jesus, “I Believe.” His Very Next Words Revealed the Battle Inside Him.
paragraphs:
A Father Told Jesus, “I Believe.” His Very Next Words Revealed the Battle Inside Him.
“Help My Unbelief” — The Prayer of a Desperate Father, a Divided Heart, and the Savior Who Is Not Frightened by Either
There are prayers you pray when everything is going well.
And then there are prayers that are ripped out of you.
Prayers without polished language.
Prayers that would never make it onto a greeting card.

Prayers spoken when your theology is still intact but your heart is shaking… when you know what you are supposed to believe, but somewhere between what you know about God and what you are actually living through, something inside you has begun to tremble.
Maybe you know that place.
You believe God is good.
But something happened.
You believe He hears prayer.
But you have been praying for a long time.
You believe He can heal.
But the diagnosis is still there.
You believe He can restore marriages.
But your house has become painfully quiet.
You believe He can bring wandering children home.
But the child you raised to know Jesus seems farther away than ever.
You believe God provides.
But the bills keep arriving.
You believe Christ forgives.
Yet sometimes, at two in the morning, your past climbs out of its grave and begins whispering your old name.
You believe.
And yet…
something inside you is still afraid.
If that contradiction has ever made you wonder whether you are a terrible Christian, there is a father in Mark chapter 9 you need to meet.
Because almost two thousand years ago, a desperate man stood before Jesus Christ and somehow managed to confess faith and unbelief in the same breath.
And Jesus did not walk away.
That may be exactly what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
Jesus did not walk away.
The story begins in chaos.
Jesus comes down from the mountain with Peter, James, and John and finds a crowd surrounding His disciples. Religious scribes are arguing with them. People are running toward Jesus.
And somewhere in that crowd is a father carrying years of private agony.
His son is suffering terribly.
Mark describes a destructive spiritual affliction involving violent convulsions. The father tells Jesus that this has been happening since the boy was a child.
Think about those words.
Since childhood.
That means this was not one horrible afternoon.
This father had history with this pain.
Years of watching.
Years of fear.
Years of wondering when the next episode would happen.
Years of being unable to fix what was destroying someone he loved.
There is a particular kind of helplessness that comes when the suffering belongs to your child.
You would take it yourself if you could.
You would trade places.
You would carry the sickness.
You would absorb the heartbreak.
You would stand between them and every demon in hell if sheer love were enough to do it.
But sometimes love has to watch what love cannot fix.
And that can break something inside a person.
The father had already brought his son to Jesus' disciples.
They could not deliver him.
Imagine what that did to the man's remaining hope.
He had come looking for help from people associated with Jesus…
and apparently left disappointed.
That detail matters.
Because sometimes people encounter the weakness of Christians and mistakenly begin wondering whether they have encountered the weakness of Christ.
But failed disciples are not a failed Savior.
Jesus was still Jesus even when His disciples could not do what needed to be done.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been wounded by Christians.
Maybe somebody represented Christ badly.
Maybe a church disappointed you.
Maybe someone quoted Scripture while living nothing like the Christ revealed in it.
Maybe you asked believers for help and walked away more wounded than when you arrived.
Do not confuse the failure of a disciple with the character of Jesus.
Look past us if you must.
But keep looking toward Him.
The father did.
When Jesus asked about the boy, the man's grief came pouring out. He explained that the destructive spirit had repeatedly thrown his son into fire and water.
Then the father said something revealing:
“If you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.”
If You can.
You can almost hear the exhaustion behind it.
This does not sound like the confidence of someone arriving with everything spiritually sorted out.
This sounds like a father whose hope has been beaten down by experience.
“If You can…”
Perhaps he had once spoken more confidently.
Perhaps years of suffering had changed his vocabulary.
Pain can do that.
At first you pray, “God is going to do this!”
Months later you whisper, “God, please…”
Eventually, after enough disappointment, some people become afraid even to hope.
Because hope makes you vulnerable.
If you expect nothing, perhaps nothing can crush you.
So you protect yourself with lowered expectations.
You still attend church.
Still say amen.
Still know the verses.
Still believe in Jesus.
But somewhere underneath all of it is a frightened little sentence:
“What if He doesn't?”
Jesus immediately places His finger on the fracture.
The Greek text of Mark 9:23 turns the father's “if You can” back toward him.
The question was never whether Christ possessed sufficient power.
The helpless father was standing before the One whose authority did not depend upon human strength.
Then comes one of the most painfully honest sentences in the entire Gospel of Mark.
The Greek text reads:
“Πιστεύω· βοήθει μου τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ.”
Pisteuō; boēthei mou tē apistia.
“I believe; help my unbelief.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
“I believe…
help my unbelief.”
The father did not pretend the contradiction was not there.
He brought the contradiction to Jesus.
And that changes everything.
Πιστεύω — pisteuō.
“I believe.”
The verb expresses believing, trusting, placing confidence in.
He had faith.
Otherwise he would not have been standing there.
But then:
βοήθει — boēthei.
“Help.”
It is an imperative plea for aid.
Not merely, “Observe my problem.”
Not, “Congratulate the part of me that believes.”
Help me.
Come to my aid.
And then the confession:
ἀπιστίᾳ — apistia.
“Unbelief.”
Distrust.
Lack of faith.
He essentially places the diseased part of his confidence directly into the hands of Christ.
“I believe You…
and I need You to help the part of me that struggles to believe You.”
What a prayer.
No performance.
No religious costume.
No pretending.
He did not wait until he possessed flawless faith before approaching Jesus.
He approached Jesus because his faith was not flawless.
That distinction can change someone's entire understanding of the Christian life.
Some of us think we must repair ourselves before approaching Christ.
Become stronger.
Become cleaner.
Stop doubting.
Stop struggling.
Fix the addiction.
Fix the thoughts.
Fix the marriage.
Fix the secret.
Fix our faith.
Then come to Jesus.
But the Gospel announces something radically different.
We come because we cannot save ourselves.
Christianity is not the story of impressive people climbing high enough to reach God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners who could never reach Him.
Jesus did not come for people who had successfully repaired themselves.
He came for sinners.
He came for the guilty.
The ashamed.
The spiritually bankrupt.
The prodigal who smells like the far country.
The disciple who promised loyalty and then denied Him.
The doubter.
The broken.
The father standing in a crowd saying, “I believe,” while simultaneously admitting, “Something inside me still doesn't.”
And maybe that father sounds uncomfortably familiar.
Because perhaps your real prayer is:
Jesus, I believe You love me…
help the part of me that still feels abandoned.
I believe You forgive…
help the part of me that keeps punishing myself.
I believe You provide…
help the part of me panicking over tomorrow.
I believe You are sovereign…
help the part of me terrified about what happens next.
I believe You can restore…
help the part of me preparing for disappointment.
I believe the Gospel…
help the part of me still listening to shame.
I believe You are enough…
help the part of me that keeps running toward things that never satisfy.
There it is.
The battle inside us.
Faith saying, “Jesus.”
Fear saying, “But what if?”
Faith saying, “He is faithful.”
Memory saying, “But remember what happened last time.”
Faith saying, “You are forgiven.”
Shame saying, “Not after what you did.”
Faith saying, “Come home.”
Pride saying, “Hide.”
And some people have spent years hiding that battle because they think admitting unbelief will offend God.
But notice what this father does.
He confesses his unbelief to the very Person he is struggling to trust.
That itself is an act of faith.
Where did he take his doubt?
To Jesus.
Where did he take his weakness?
To Jesus.
Where did he take his child?
To Jesus.
Where did he take the part of himself that was spiritually malfunctioning?
To Jesus.
That is where the Gospel keeps bringing us.
Not deeper into ourselves.
Not into motivational self-salvation.
Not into pretending.
To Christ.
Jesus then rebukes the unclean spirit.
The boy is violently convulsed and becomes so still that many conclude he is dead.
For one terrifying moment, imagine being that father.
You came asking Jesus to save your son.
Jesus intervened.
And now your child looks dead.
Have you ever obeyed God only for circumstances to initially look worse?
Have you ever finally surrendered something to Jesus and then watched everything appear to collapse?
This is where we are tempted to judge Christ's work before Christ has finished working.
The crowd looked at the boy and said, in effect:
“It is over.”
But Jesus was not finished.
Mark tells us that Jesus took the boy by the hand and raised him.
The hands of Jesus changed the conclusion.
People saw death.
Jesus reached down.
People thought the story was finished.
Jesus reached down.
People had already formed their verdict.
Jesus reached down.
And the boy stood up.
That is not merely sentimental imagery.
It points us toward the center of Christian hope.
Because ultimately our faith does not rest upon the promise that every earthly circumstance will end exactly as we desire.
The Gospel promises something greater.
Jesus Christ Himself entered our death.
The sinless Son of God went to the cross bearing sin, suffering under judgment, shedding His blood for sinners.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, Jesus Christ rose bodily from the grave.
Christian hope therefore does not rest on positive thinking.
It rests on a resurrected Person.
The Christian can stare into darkness and still have hope because our Savior has already walked through a grave and come out alive.
That does not mean Christians never grieve.
It does not mean every illness is healed in this life.
It does not mean sufficient faith guarantees money, success, comfort, or whatever outcome we demand.
Mark 9 is not a blank check for manipulating God.
Faith is not spiritual currency with which we purchase miracles.
Faith has an object.
Jesus Christ.
The power in this story was not the father's ability to generate enough psychological certainty.
The power belonged to Jesus.
That is precisely why the father's confession is so beautiful.
His hope was not:
“My faith is powerful.”
His cry was:
“Help me.”
The strength of Christianity has never been the perfection of the believer.
It is Christ.
And perhaps this is where this article stops being about an unnamed father from the first century and becomes painfully personal.
What are you hiding behind “I'm okay”?
What unbelief are you afraid to confess?
What disappointment with God have you buried beneath Christian vocabulary?
What prayer have you almost stopped praying?
What wound made you suspicious of hope?
What secret sin keeps telling you that you cannot come back?
What have you been trying desperately to repair before allowing Jesus to see it?
He already sees it.
The question is whether you will bring it into the light.
Biblical faith is not pretending darkness does not exist.
Faith brings the darkness to Christ.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it only needs to be true.
“Jesus, I believe.
Help my unbelief.”
If you have sinned, do not merely rename your sin as a struggle and leave it untouched.
Repent.
Turn toward Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Bring into the light what darkness has taught you to protect.
Grace does not mean sin does not matter.
Grace means sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so astonishing that guilty people who come to Him can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and made new.
That is the scandal of grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left with which to impress anybody.
Grace met him while he was dying.
And this desperate father brought Jesus faith tangled together with unbelief.
Christ did not demand that he return when the knot was untangled.
He met him there.
Again and again.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have a scandal too.
Not necessarily one anybody knows about.
Maybe yours exists entirely behind your smile.
The secret addiction.
The resentment.
The compromise.
The marriage barely surviving behind beautiful Facebook photographs.
The private anxiety underneath public worship.
The Bible collecting dust while Christian posts continue appearing on your timeline.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The bitterness you justified.
The faith you pretend is stronger than it actually is.
Jesus is not asking you to impress Him.
He is calling you into truth.
And truth sometimes sounds like:
“I believe…
but help me.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a spiritual answer.
Be honest.
Not because typing words earns anything from God.
It doesn't.
Christ cannot be purchased by engagement.
But there is something powerful about refusing to hide and allowing other struggling believers to discover that they are not alone.
Let believers who see it pray with you.

If Christ has already carried you through a season when your faith almost collapsed, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the encouragement another exhausted person desperately needed tonight.
And think of one person whose faith has been wounded.
Not ten random people.
One person.
The friend quietly questioning God.
The mother exhausted from praying for her child.
The father carrying a burden nobody sees.
The Christian who still attends church but privately wonders whether God has forgotten them.
The prodigal who assumes he has gone too far.
“I believe…
help my unbelief.”
Let truth find them there.
Because today you may be strong enough to send it to somebody else.
Tomorrow you may be the one who needs to read it again.

We want this ministry to keep putting Christ-centered Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment in front of people living in a world drowning in noise.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. Salvation cannot be bought. Grace cannot be bought.
We support Gospel ministry because we love Christ, love people, and want truth to travel farther.
But before you leave, remember the father.
Remember his son.
Remember the crowd.
Remember the disciples who could not fix the situation.
Remember the exhausted words:
“If You can…”
Remember Jesus turning the man's attention away from the imagined limitation in Christ.
And remember the cry that followed:
“Πιστεύω· βοήθει μου τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ.”
“I believe; help my unbelief.”
Maybe you thought mature faith meant never struggling.
Maybe mature faith sometimes looks like knowing exactly where to take the struggle.
To Jesus.
You don't have to pretend your unbelief is faith.
You don't have to call fear courage.
You don't have to hide your questions beneath religious vocabulary.
Bring them to Christ.
And if you have wandered into sin, bring that too.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
The same Jesus who received desperate people in the Gospels still calls sinners to Himself through the Gospel.
Your confidence is not that you have held onto Him perfectly.
Your confidence is that Christ is a sufficient Savior.
So tonight, when your heart whispers:
“I believe…”
and another voice immediately answers:
“But I'm afraid…”
do what that father did.
Finish the sentence in the presence of Jesus.
“Help me.”
And comment before you leave.
“Jesus, help my unbelief.”
Let that become more than a comment.
Let it become your prayer.

Because perhaps the most dangerous lie unbelief ever told you was that you needed stronger faith before you could come closer to Jesus—when all along, the trembling part of you was exactly what you needed to bring Him.
The father brought Jesus a son he could not rescue and a faith he could not repair—and discovered that Jesus was sufficient for both.
